etymology: From Reformed (of the Protestant Reformation) + doctrine; the body of confessional teaching recovered at the Reformation.
biblical_def: Reformed doctrine is the body of biblical teaching recovered and confessed at the Protestant Reformation and set down in the great confessions—the Westminster Standards, the 1689 London Baptist Confession, the Three Forms of Unity. Its heart is the five solas: that salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, on the authority of Scripture alone, to the glory of God alone. It confesses the sovereignty of God in all things, especially in salvation; the total depravity of fallen man; the unconditional election of God’s people according to His good pleasure; the definite atonement of Christ for His own; the effectual call of the Spirit; and the perseverance of the saints—the doctrines of grace summarized in the Canons of Dort. It holds the covenant as the framework of God’s dealings, the regulative principle in worship, and the supreme authority of the inspired and sufficient Scriptures. Reformed doctrine is not the invention of Calvin or any man, but the recovery of the gospel of the apostles and of Augustine, against the works-righteousness and accumulated corruptions of late-medieval Rome. The dictionary honors Reformed doctrine as the fullest confessional expression of biblical Christianity, exalting the sovereign grace of God in the salvation of sinners, casting man wholly upon the mercy of God in Christ, and rendering all glory to God alone—the system of truth this whole work is written to commend and defend.
webster_summary: The body of biblical teaching recovered at the Reformation—the five solas and the doctrines of grace—exalting God’s sovereign grace in the salvation of sinners.
webster_full: REFORMED DOCTRINE, the biblical teaching recovered at the Reformation.
Its heart: grace, faith, Christ, Scripture, and the glory of God alone.
Confesses God’s sovereignty, total depravity, and unconditional election.
Definite atonement, effectual call, perseverance—the doctrines of grace.
Not Calvin’s invention, but the recovered gospel of the apostles.

corruption_summary: Reformed doctrine is caricatured as cold determinism or dismissed as Calvin’s novelty; it is the recovered gospel of sovereign grace, warm with the love of God in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two caricatures dog Reformed doctrine. The first paints it as cold philosophical determinism—God as an arbitrary tyrant, men as puppets, evangelism as pointless. But this slanders a doctrine whose very heart is the warm, free, conquering love of God toward unworthy sinners, and which has fueled the greatest missions and the tenderest pastoral care. The second dismisses it as Calvin’s sixteenth-century novelty, forgetting that its substance was confessed by Augustine against Pelagius and by Paul against the Judaizers.

The principle to recover is that Reformed doctrine is simply the gospel of sovereign grace, drawn from Scripture and exalting God. Salvation is of the LORD (Jon 2:9); it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy (Rom 9:16); by grace are ye saved through faith, and that not of yourselves (Eph 2:8). The whole system bends to one end: that of Him, and through Him, and to Him are all things, to whom be glory for ever (Rom 11:36). Far from making God a tyrant, it casts the helpless sinner wholly on His mercy in Christ and renders Him all the glory—the very posture of the gospel.
roots_summary: Reformed + doctrine; the biblical teaching recovered at the Reformation—the solas and the doctrines of grace—exalting God’s sovereign grace in salvation.

The five solas are the heart of the gospel recovered at the Reformation.
Far from cold determinism, it casts the sinner on the mercy of God in Christ.

etymology: From Reformed + catechism (Greek katecheo, to instruct by word of mouth); the question-and-answer manuals of Reformed instruction.
biblical_def: The Reformed catechisms are the question-and-answer manuals by which the Reformed churches have instructed their people, young and old, in the faith. Chief among them are the Heidelberg Catechism, with its tender opening on the believer’s only comfort in life and death, that he is not his own but belongs to his faithful Saviour Jesus Christ; the Westminster Shorter and Larger Catechisms, with the great first answer that man’s chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy Him for ever; and the Baptist Catechism, which adapts the Westminster for confessional Baptists. Catechizing follows the apostolic pattern of teaching the form of sound words and the first principles of the oracles of God, and the ancient practice of the church, which from the earliest days instructed converts and covenant children in the rudiments of the faith before the Lord’s table. The catechisms summarize the whole counsel of God—what we are to believe concerning God, and what duty God requires of man—in a form to be learned, recited, and pressed upon the heart. The dictionary honors the Reformed catechisms as a chief instrument of the church’s teaching office, a means of grounding the people in sound doctrine against the winds of error, and a treasure for the family and the church; and it laments the widespread neglect of catechizing, which leaves a generation untaught in the very rudiments of the faith.
webster_summary: The question-and-answer manuals of Reformed instruction—Heidelberg, Westminster, the Baptist Catechism—grounding the church in sound doctrine and the duty God requires.
webster_full: REFORMED CATECHISMS, the question-and-answer manuals of Reformed instruction.
Heidelberg: the believer’s only comfort is that he belongs to Christ.
Westminster: man’s chief end is to glorify God and enjoy Him for ever.
The Baptist Catechism adapts the Westminster for confessional Baptists.
A chief instrument of grounding the church in sound doctrine.

Heb 5:12

For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.
Luk 1:4

corruption_summary: Catechizing is dismissed as cold rote or sterile tradition; Scripture commends the diligent teaching of sound words and first principles to old and young.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the modern dismissal of catechizing as cold rote learning, dead formality, or sterile tradition that quenches living faith. This judgment mistakes the form for the substance. The catechisms are not meant to replace heart-religion but to ground it; the memorized answer becomes a lamp the believer carries through life, a settled summary of truth to steady him when error blows and trials come. Many a saint has found the catechism’s words on his lips in the hour of death.

The principle to recover is the duty and blessing of catechetical instruction. Scripture commands the diligent teaching of God’s truth to children (Deu 6:7), the holding fast of the form of sound words (2 Tim 1:13), and the grounding of believers in the first principles of the oracles of God (Heb 5:12); Luke wrote his Gospel that Theophilus might know the certainty of the things wherein he had been instructed—catechized (Luke 1:4). The neglect of catechizing has left a generation untaught in the very rudiments of the faith, easy prey to every error. The Reformed catechisms remain a chief instrument of the church’s teaching office, a treasure for family and church, to be recovered, not despised.

etymology: From plenary (full) + verbal (of the words) + inspiration (in-breathing); the doctrine that all the words of Scripture are God-breathed.
biblical_def: Plenary verbal inspiration is the doctrine that the whole of Scripture (plenary, full), and the very words of Scripture (verbal), are inspired—breathed out by God. It holds that the Holy Ghost so moved and superintended the human authors that what they wrote, down to the words, is the word of God, true and without error in the original autographs, and authoritative in all it affirms. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, theopneustos, God-breathed; holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. The inspiration is plenary: it extends to all the Scripture, not merely to certain doctrines or moral teachings, but to history, prophecy, and every part. And it is verbal: it reaches to the words themselves, for the Lord and His apostles built arguments on single words and the very tenses of verbs. This does not make the human authors mere pens; the Spirit used their minds, styles, and circumstances, yet so governed them that the result is wholly the word of God and wholly their word, without error. The dictionary honors plenary verbal inspiration as the church’s confession of the nature of Scripture, the foundation of its authority and sufficiency, against every doctrine that would make the Bible merely contain the word of God, or err in its words, or inspire only its religious sentiments. The Scripture cannot be broken, for it is the very breath of God.
webster_summary: The doctrine that all Scripture, down to its words, is breathed out by God—true, without error, and authoritative—the holy authors moved by the Holy Ghost.
webster_full: PLENARY VERBAL INSPIRATION, that all the words of Scripture are God-breathed.
Plenary: the whole of Scripture, not select doctrines only.
Verbal: the very words, on which Christ and the apostles built arguments.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God (2Ti 3:16).
Holy men spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost (2Pe 1:21).
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
Mat 5:18

If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
corruption_summary: Inspiration is reduced to the Bible merely containing God’s word, or inspiring only its sentiments; Scripture testifies that its very words are breathed out by God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the liberal-critical reduction. The chief corruption, flowing from modern liberal and critical scholarship, denies plenary verbal inspiration in various ways: that the Bible merely contains the word of God amid human error; that only its religious or moral teachings are inspired, not its history or its words; that inspiration means only an elevated human insight, not the breathing-out of God. Each of these makes the church, the scholar, or the reader the judge of which words are God’s, and so dissolves the authority of Scripture into the authority of man.

The principle to recover is the Bible’s own testimony to itself. All scripture is given by inspiration of God—theopneustos, God-breathed (2 Tim 3:16); the prophecy came not by the will of man, but holy men spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost (2 Pet 1:21). The Lord pressed inspiration down to the jot and tittle, the smallest stroke of the law (Matt 5:18), and declared that the scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). This is plenary—the whole—and verbal—the very words. To confess it is to bow before the Bible as the very breath of God, true, authoritative, and sufficient; to deny it is to set up a Bible within the Bible, judged by the spirit of the age.
roots_summary: Plenary (full) + verbal (of the words) + inspiration (God-breathing); the doctrine that all the words of Scripture are breathed out by God, true and authoritative.

etymology: From presence + God; the manifold ways in which God is present to His creation and His people.
biblical_def: The presence of God is the manifold way in which God, who fills heaven and earth, is present to His creation and especially to His people. Scripture distinguishes several senses, all true at once. God is everywhere present by His essence and power, His omnipresence, so that no man can flee from His Spirit nor hide from His face; whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? He is present in judgment to the wicked, before whom the day of the LORD is a terror, who shall be punished with destruction from the presence of the Lord. And He is present in grace and blessing to His people—a special, covenantal, saving presence, promised in the words, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee, and supremely in Christ, Immanuel, God with us, and by the indwelling Spirit who makes the believer a temple of God. The fulness of this presence is the believer’s heaven: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore; and the hope of the saints is to behold His face in righteousness and be satisfied. The dictionary honors the presence of God as the great theme of the believer’s life and hope—dreadful to the impenitent, the sum of all blessing to the redeemed—distinguishing His omnipresence, which none escapes, from His gracious presence, which is the portion of His covenant people, and pointing to the day when they shall dwell in His presence and see Him face to face.
webster_summary: The manifold presence of God—everywhere by His essence, in judgment to the wicked, in saving grace to His people—the sum of the believer’s blessing and hope.
webster_full: PRESENCE OF GOD, the manifold way God is present to His creation.
Omnipresent by essence: none can flee from His presence (Psa 139:7).
Present in judgment to the wicked, a terror in the day of the LORD.
Present in saving grace to His people: I will never leave thee.
In His presence is fulness of joy for evermore (Psa 16:11).
scriptures: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;
corruption_summary: God’s presence is reduced to a vague feeling, or His omnipresence confused with His saving presence; Scripture distinguishes the senses and exalts His gracious presence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the presence of God. The first reduces it to a vague spiritual feeling—a sense of the numinous, a mood of worship—detached from the God who is and the truths He has revealed. The second confuses the senses of His presence, blurring His omnipresence, which fills all and which the wicked cannot escape, with His gracious saving presence, which is the special portion of His covenant people. To collapse these is to promise the comfort of His nearness to those who are in fact under His judgment.

The principle to recover is the careful biblical distinction, and the exaltation of His gracious presence. God is everywhere by His essence; none can flee from His Spirit (Psa 139:7). To the wicked this presence is terror, for they shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord (2 Thess 1:9). But to His people He is present in covenant grace: I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee (Heb 13:5); He is Immanuel, God with us, and dwells in them by His Spirit. This gracious presence is the believer’s heaven begun: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore (Psa 16:11). The presence none can escape is the dread of the lost; the presence freely given is the joy of the saved.
roots_summary: Presence + God; the manifold presence of God—omnipresent, judicial, and gracious—the dread of the wicked and the sum of the believer’s blessing.

etymology: From throne + God; the seat and symbol of the LORD’s sovereign rule over all things.
biblical_def: The throne of God is the seat and symbol of the LORD’s sovereign, eternal rule over all that He has made. The LORD hath prepared his throne in the heavens; and his kingdom ruleth over all. Heaven is His throne, and the earth His footstool; He sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers. The prophets beheld it: Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and the seraphim crying, Holy, holy, holy; Ezekiel saw the likeness of a throne above the firmament; Daniel saw the Ancient of days sit, His throne like the fiery flame; and John saw a throne set in heaven, and One that sat thereon, encircled by a rainbow and worshipped by the living creatures and the elders day and night. The throne is a throne of holiness, of justice, and of grace—justice and judgment are the habitation of His throne—and to it the believer is bidden come boldly, that he may find grace to help, for the throne of judgment has become, through Christ, a throne of grace. From the throne proceeds the river of the water of life; before it the redeemed shall stand and serve. The dictionary honors the throne of God as the great symbol of His sovereignty, holiness, and grace—the seat from which He governs all things, judges all men, and dispenses mercy to His people through the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne.
webster_summary: The seat and symbol of the LORD’s sovereign, eternal rule; a throne of holiness, justice, and—through Christ—grace, to which the believer comes boldly.
webster_full: THRONE OF GOD, the seat and symbol of the LORD’s sovereign rule.
His throne is in the heavens; His kingdom ruleth over all (Psa 103:19).
Beheld by Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and John in glory.
A throne of holiness and justice; justice is its habitation.
Through Christ, a throne of grace, to which we come boldly (Heb 4:16).
scriptures: The LORD hath prepared his throne in the heavens; and his kingdom ruleth over all.
Isa 6:1
In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.
Heb 4:16

Rev 4:2
And immediately I was in the spirit: and, behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one sat on the throne.
corruption_summary: The throne of God is reduced to mere imagery or emptied of His real sovereignty; Scripture sets it as the seat of His holy rule, justice, and saving grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the modern instinct to treat the throne of God as mere poetic imagery, a figure emptied of its reality—as though God did not truly reign, or His sovereignty were a metaphor we may take or leave. But the prophets and apostles beheld the throne as the most solid of realities: Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up (Isa 6:1), and John saw a throne set in heaven, and One that sat upon it (Rev 4:2). The throne is the symbol of a rule that is actual, absolute, and eternal.

The principle to recover is the union of sovereignty, holiness, justice, and grace in the throne. The LORD hath prepared His throne in the heavens, and His kingdom ruleth over all (Psa 103:19)—nothing is outside His government. It is a throne of holiness, before which the seraphim veil their faces and cry, Holy, holy, holy; and a throne of justice, for justice and judgment are its habitation. Yet—wonder of the gospel—through the blood of Christ the throne of judgment has become for the believer a throne of grace, to which he is bidden come boldly, that he may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:16). The throne that the wicked must dread is the very throne where the saint finds mercy.
roots_summary: Throne + God; the seat of the LORD’s sovereign, holy, just rule, become through Christ a throne of grace to which the believer comes boldly.

etymology: From divine + will; the will of God, distinguished by the theologians into His secret and revealed will.
biblical_def: The divine will is the will of God, by which He purposes and accomplishes all things according to His own good pleasure. The theologians distinguish two aspects, both taught in Scripture. There is the secret or decretive will of God—His eternal, sovereign, and unchangeable purpose, by which He has foreordained whatsoever comes to pass; this will is always accomplished, for who hath resisted His will? He doeth according to His will in the army of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth, and none can stay His hand. And there is the revealed or preceptive will of God—His commandments, what He has made known of our duty in His word; this will is often disobeyed by sinners, for men break His commandments daily, yet it is the rule of our obedience. The secret will is the rule of God’s actions; the revealed will is the rule of ours. We are not to pry into the secret things, which belong unto the LORD, but to do the things that are revealed, which belong to us and to our children. The distinction guards against great errors: it preserves the sovereignty of God, who accomplishes His whole purpose, and the responsibility of man, who is bound by the commands; and it forbids us to excuse our sin by appeal to the decree, or to charge God with the evil men do. The dictionary honors the doctrine of the divine will as a key to the harmony of Scripture: God ordains all things by His secret will, and yet sincerely commands all men by His revealed will, and is the author of no man’s sin.
webster_summary: The will of God, distinguished into His secret will (the decree that ordains all) and His revealed will (His commands, the rule of our duty); the key to sovereignty and responsibility.
webster_full: DIVINE WILL, the will of God, by which He purposes and accomplishes all.
The secret or decretive will: His eternal purpose, always accomplished.
The revealed or preceptive will: His commands, the rule of our duty.
The secret things belong to God; the revealed, to us (Deu 29:29).
Guards both the sovereignty of God and the responsibility of man.
scriptures: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
Dan 4:35

And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?
Eph 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication:
corruption_summary: God’s will is flattened to one thing, pitting sovereignty against command; Scripture’s distinction of secret and revealed will upholds both, excusing no sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the flattening of the divine will into a single undistinguished thing, which then pits the sovereignty of God against His commands. Some seize the decree to deny that God truly commands or sincerely calls all men; others seize the commands to deny that God ordains all things; and the impenitent seize the decree to excuse their sin—if God willed it, how am I guilty? The confusion breeds error on every side.

The principle to recover is the biblical distinction of God’s secret and revealed will. By His secret will He worketh all things after the counsel of His own will (Eph 1:11) and doeth according to His will in heaven and earth, and none can stay His hand (Dan 4:35); this is the rule of His actions, and it is always done. By His revealed will He commands our duty—this is the will of God, even your sanctification (1 Thess 4:3); this is the rule of our obedience, and it is often broken by sinners. The secret things belong to God; the revealed belong to us, that we may do them (Deu 29:29). The distinction upholds both God’s sovereignty and man’s responsibility, forbids the sinner to hide behind the decree, and clears God of the evil men do: He ordains all, commands the good, and is the author of no man’s sin.
roots_summary: Divine + will; the will of God in its secret (decretive) and revealed (preceptive) aspects, upholding His sovereignty and man’s responsibility.
roots_lines: Divine will — the will of God, secret and revealed.
Secret will: His decree, worked after the counsel of His will (Eph 1:11).
Revealed will: His commands, the rule of our duty (1Th 4:3).
The secret things belong to God; the revealed, to us (Deu 29:29).
Upholds God’s sovereignty and man’s responsibility alike.
usage: The divine will is distinguished into God’s secret and revealed will.
By His secret will He worketh all things after the counsel of His own will.
The secret things belong to the LORD; the revealed, to us, that we may obey.

etymology: From Deuteronomy 29:29; the distinction between the secret things of God and the things revealed.
biblical_def: Secret and revealed names the great distinction set down by Moses: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law. There are things God has kept to Himself—the depths of His counsel, the times and seasons in His own power, the reasons of His providences, the identity of the elect, the day and hour of the end—which He has not revealed, and into which it is not ours to pry; the secret things belong to Him. And there are things He has made known in His word—His character, His commands, the way of salvation in Christ, all that we need to believe and to do—which belong to us and to our children, and which we are bound to receive and obey. The distinction is a charter of both humility and diligence: humility, not to intrude into what God has hidden, nor to demand answers He has not given, but to say with Paul, O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments; and diligence, to study and obey all that He has revealed, leaving nothing of His word neglected. The dictionary honors this distinction as a fence and a guide: it fences curiosity from the secret counsel of God, and it directs the whole heart to the revealed will, that we may do all the words of His law, content to trust where we cannot trace, and bound to obey all that He has spoken.
webster_summary: Moses’ distinction (Deu 29:29) between the secret things that belong to God and the revealed things that belong to us; a charter of humility and of diligent obedience.
webster_full: SECRET AND REVEALED, Moses’ distinction in Deuteronomy 29:29.
The secret things—God’s counsel, times, reasons—belong to Him.
The revealed things—His word, commands, salvation—belong to us.
Forbids prying into what God has hidden.
Binds us to obey all that He has revealed.
scriptures: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Act 1:7
And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.
Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
corruption_summary: Men intrude into God’s secrets or neglect His revealed will; the distinction fences curiosity and binds the heart to obey all that God has spoken.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite faults transgress this distinction. The first intrudes into the secret things—demanding to know the day of the end, the reasons behind God’s painful providences, the names in the book of life, the resolution of mysteries He has not opened—and so breeds speculation, date-setting, and a restless, faithless curiosity. The second neglects the revealed things, leaving much of God’s plain word unstudied and unobeyed while the mind chases hidden matters. Both forget the boundary Moses drew.

The principle to recover is the boundary itself: the secret things belong unto the LORD our God; but the revealed things belong unto us and to our children, that we may do all the words of this law (Deu 29:29). Toward the hidden counsel of God the right posture is humble adoration—O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are His judgments (Rom 11:33)—and contentment to trust where we cannot trace, knowing it is not for us to know the times the Father has kept in His own power (Acts 1:7). Toward the revealed will the right posture is diligent obedience, searching out the matter God has set before us (Pro 25:2). To honor both is wisdom: to trust the secret, and to obey the revealed.
roots_summary: From Deuteronomy 29:29; the distinction between the secret things that belong to God and the revealed things that belong to us, a charter of humility and obedience.
roots_lines: Secret and revealed — Moses’ distinction (Deu 29:29).

Toward the revealed: diligent obedience, to do all His words.
usage: The secret things belong to the LORD; the revealed, to us and our children.

etymology: From the biblical phrase, the good pleasure of God’s will (Eph 1:5, 9); His free, sovereign, gracious purpose.
biblical_def: The good pleasure of God is His free, sovereign, and gracious purpose, the unconstrained delight of His will, which is the ultimate ground of all His works of creation, providence, and redemption. The phrase recurs in the Scriptures of election and salvation: God predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will; He has made known the mystery of His will, according to His good pleasure which He hath purposed in Himself; and the Lord rejoiced, saying, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes: even so, Father; for so it seemed good in thy sight. The good pleasure of God means that the reason for His choice lies not in the creature—not in foreseen faith, worth, or works—but in Himself, in the free delight of His own will. It is the deepest answer to every question of why God saves whom He saves: because it pleased Him. Yet His good pleasure is not arbitrary caprice but the delight of infinite wisdom, holiness, and love. The dictionary honors the good pleasure of God as the bedrock of grace: that salvation springs from the free, sovereign delight of God, who works in His people both to will and to do of His good pleasure, and that the Father’s good pleasure is to give His little flock the kingdom.
webster_summary: The free, sovereign, gracious purpose of God—the delight of His will—the ground of election and salvation, lying not in the creature but in God Himself.
webster_full: GOOD PLEASURE, the free, sovereign, gracious purpose of God’s will.

The reason for His choice lies in Himself, not in the creature.
Not arbitrary caprice, but the delight of infinite wisdom and love.
It is the Father’s good pleasure to give His flock the kingdom (Luk 12:32).

corruption_summary: God’s good pleasure is recast as arbitrary tyranny, or denied so His choice rests on the creature; Scripture grounds election in His free, wise, gracious delight.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the good pleasure of God. The first recoils from it as arbitrary tyranny—as though to ground salvation in God’s free delight made Him a capricious despot choosing without reason. But His good pleasure is the delight of infinite wisdom, holiness, and love, never bare caprice; it is good as well as free. The second error, fearing the sovereignty, locates the reason for God’s choice in the creature—in foreseen faith, worth, or works—and so empties grace of its freeness.

The principle to recover is that the ground of election lies in God Himself, in the free, sovereign, gracious pleasure of His will. He predestinated us according to the good pleasure of His will (Eph 1:5); the Lord rejoiced that the Father had hidden these things from the wise and revealed them unto babes, for so it seemed good in His sight (Matt 11:26). This is the deepest answer to why God saves whom He saves: because it pleased Him. Far from a terror, it is the believer’s sweetest comfort, for the same good pleasure that chose him now works in him both to will and to do (Phil 2:13), and it is the Father’s good pleasure to give His little flock the kingdom (Luke 12:32). Grace rests on God’s delight, and therefore cannot fail.
roots_summary: From Ephesians 1; the good pleasure of God’s will, His free, sovereign, gracious delight, the ground of election lying in Himself, not the creature.

etymology: From surety (one who guarantees another’s debt) + covenant; the title of Christ as guarantor of the better covenant (Heb 7:22).
biblical_def: The surety of the covenant is a title of the Lord Jesus Christ, the one who stands as guarantor of the better covenant, undertaking and securing all its terms on behalf of His people. A surety is one who pledges himself to answer for another’s debt or obligation, becoming responsible in his stead. The Scripture says, By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament. As surety of the covenant of grace, Christ undertook from eternity to satisfy all the broken law’s demands against His people—to bear their debt, to fulfil the righteousness they owed, and to secure for them every promised blessing. He answered for them on both sides of the covenant: meeting God’s justice by His perfect obedience and atoning death, and guaranteeing to His people the certain accomplishment of all the covenant’s promises—pardon, adoption, sanctification, and glory. Because the surety is divine and His undertaking cannot fail, the covenant He guarantees is ordered in all things and sure, an everlasting covenant that shall not be broken. The believer’s salvation therefore rests not on his own keeping but on the suretyship of Christ, who has paid the debt and pledged the inheritance. The dictionary honors Christ as the surety of the covenant—the great guarantor who answered for His people’s debt and secured their every blessing—the ground of the believer’s assurance, that the covenant cannot fail, for its surety is the Son of God.
webster_summary: A title of Christ, the guarantor of the better covenant, who answered for His people’s debt and secured their every blessing; the ground of the believer’s assurance.

corruption_summary: Salvation is made to rest on the believer’s own covenant-keeping; Scripture grounds the covenant’s certainty in Christ the surety, who cannot fail.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the legalizing instinct that makes the believer’s salvation rest, finally, on his own covenant-keeping—as though the new covenant were a bargain the Christian must perform to secure, and his standing hung on the steadiness of his obedience. This forgets that the covenant of grace has a surety, and turns the gospel back into a covenant of works the sinner cannot keep.

The principle to recover is the suretyship of Christ. By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament (Heb 7:22): He pledged Himself to answer for His people’s whole debt and to secure their every blessing. He met the justice of God by His obedience and death, redeeming the transgressions under the first covenant, that the called might receive the promised eternal inheritance (Heb 9:15); and He guarantees to His people the certain accomplishment of all the covenant’s promises. Because the surety is the Son of God, who cannot fail, the covenant is ordered in all things, and sure (2 Sam 23:5). The believer’s assurance rests not on his own keeping but on Christ’s suretyship; the Father gave Him for a covenant of the people (Isa 42:6), and what the surety has undertaken, He will surely accomplish.

etymology: From Latin ubique, everywhere; the Lutheran doctrine that Christ’s human body is omnipresent, framed to defend consubstantiation.
biblical_def: The ubiquity of Christ’s body is the Lutheran doctrine that the human body of Christ, by virtue of its union with His divine nature, partakes of the divine attribute of omnipresence, and so is or may be present everywhere—a teaching framed chiefly to defend the bodily presence of Christ in, with, and under the bread of the Lord’s Supper (consubstantiation). The Reformed churches reject this doctrine as contrary to Scripture and to the Chalcedonian definition of Christ’s two natures. Scripture teaches that Christ has a true human body, like ours in all things save sin, and a true human body is by nature local, occupying one place; it was born, grew, was crucified, rose, and ascended bodily, and the angels declared, He is not here: for he is risen. He was received up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, whom the heavens must receive until the times of restitution of all things—words that locate His body in heaven, not everywhere. The two natures are united in one Person without confusion: the divine remains divine, omnipresent; the human remains human, local; the properties of one nature are not transferred to the other. To make Christ’s body ubiquitous is to confound the natures, swallowing up His true humanity in His deity. The dictionary names the ubiquity of Christ’s body as a Lutheran error, framed to prop consubstantiation, which violates both the plain teaching of Scripture on Christ’s ascended body and the Chalcedonian confession of His two unconfused natures.
webster_summary: The Lutheran doctrine that Christ’s human body is omnipresent, framed to defend consubstantiation; rejected as confounding His two natures and denying His ascended, local body.
webster_full: UBIQUITY OF CHRIST'S BODY, the Lutheran doctrine of His body’s omnipresence.

corruption_summary: The doctrine of ubiquity confounds Christ’s two natures to prop consubstantiation; Scripture confesses His true, local human body, ascended and seated in heaven.
corruption_paragraphs: The ubiquity of Christ’s body is itself the corruption this entry names: a Lutheran doctrine, devised to defend the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper, which teaches that His human body partakes of the divine omnipresence and so is everywhere. The error springs from a true premise wrongly applied—the union of the two natures in one Person—by transferring the property of the divine nature (omnipresence) to the human nature, which is precisely what the Chalcedonian definition forbids: the natures are united without confusion or change. To make the body ubiquitous is to swallow up Christ’s true humanity in His deity, leaving Him not truly man.

Scripture holds the line. Christ took a true human body, made like unto His brethren in all things, that He might be a merciful high priest (Heb 2:17); and a true human body is local, occupying one place. The angel said of that body, He is not here: for he is risen (Matt 28:6); He was taken up into heaven (Acts 1:11), whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things (Acts 3:21). His body is therefore in heaven, at the right hand of God, not everywhere. The Reformed confess His real spiritual presence in the Supper by the Holy Ghost to the believing soul, without dragging His body down from heaven or stretching it everywhere. The ubiquity doctrine, framed to prop consubstantiation, must be refused as contrary both to the Scriptures on His ascended body and to the confession of His two unconfounded natures.
roots_summary: Latin ubique, everywhere; the Lutheran doctrine of Christ’s body’s omnipresence, framed to defend consubstantiation, rejected for confounding His two natures.
